newsitem.title: DUBAI: U.S., Gulf Arabs out of step over Israel.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Gulf Arabs out of step over Israel.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen talked tough against Iran during his first Gulf tour but Washington's allies on the Arab side of the volatile region had other issues on their minds.

The recurrent American theme of Iran as the biggest threat to the security of oil exports to the West struck a chord with Gulf Arab leaders who have watched nervously as the Islamic republic flexes its military muscle in the strategic waterway.

But Gulf Arab leaders seized on Cohen's familiarisation visit as an opportunity to deliver a rare public rebuke to the United States over a controversial vote in Washington affirming Jerusalem as Israel's undivided capital.

The House of Representatives resolution angered Arabs at a time when relations between Israelis and Palestinians are in crisis over construction of a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem, captured by Israel in the 1967 Six-Day War.
Palestinians consider the eastern part of the city, annexed by Israel, as capital of a future state.
Vocal criticism of U.S. policy in the Middle East and support for the Jewish state followed Cohen as he toured Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates and Oman.
The fact that the U.S. resolution was non-binding and did not reflect Clinton administration policy seemed not to matter.

Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil exporter and Washington's most significant ally in the Gulf, condemned the vote as an obstacle to the Middle East peace process and said it violated the foundations of peace.
"Kingdom flays vote on Jerusalem" blared a bold-type headline in the Saudi Gazette -- rare sentiment for any newspaper in the closely-controlled pro-American kingdom.

The cabinet of Kuwait, grateful for liberation from Iraqi occupation forces by a U.S.-led military coalition in the 1991 Gulf War, expressed regret and concern and said the vote was a hindrance to the peace process.
Bahrain's advisory Shura Council denounced it as threatening the entire peace process and said it violated international legitimacy and was a blow to the feelings of Arabs and Moslems.
The UAE said the vote damaged the peace process and cast doubt over Washington's neutrality in that process.

UAE President Sheikh Zaid bin Sultan al-Naharan, the Gulf's elder statesman, told Cohen the United States must bring Israel into line and urge it to commit itself to the accords which had already been signed between previous Israeli governments and the Palestinians.

Gulf News daily said on Thursday Cohen's remarks about Iran reflected Washington's obsession and said it was crucial that President Bill Clinton avoided repeating the mistakes of his first term in office by reviewing Washington's totally unproductive policy of dual containment against Iran and Iraq.

"The U.S. cannot hope to keep the long term goodwill of the Gulf Arab countries, which it sees as its allies, if it continues to overlook Israel's outrageous treatment of Palestinians," the newspaper said.

"For that matter, the U.S. policy of dual containment of Iran and Iraq is at cross purposes with its reliance on the goodwill of the Gulf Arabs. Political schizophrenia is a luxury that the U.S. cannot afford."

Cohen did not go to the sixth Gulf Arab oil-producer Qatar, but that country's emir was in Washington where he voiced fears of a possible showdown "at any moment" between the United States and Iran which he said would harm all countries in the region.

Cohen eased tension by saying the United States was not headed for a clash unless Iran started it but pledging at the same time that the large force of American troops, warships and warplanes stationed in the Gulf region would stay indefinitely.
Iran said on Thursday Cohen's Gulf visit aimed at creating tension in the region.
It called his comments against Iran part of Washington's "poisonous propaganda by the U.S. against the Islamic republic of Iran aimed at creating a sense of anxiety in the region".
Tehran says Washington falsely accuses it of threatening regional security in order to scare its Gulf Arab allies into buying ever more American weapons.

Tehran Times newspaper said on Thursday that Cohen, in his meetings with Gulf leaders, justified the need for a continued U.S. military presence in the region, the necessity of allocating new budgets for U.S. weapons purchases, and instilled fear of Iran in their hearts.
